other_side: Zitron, writing the day before, does not address the dinner-table idea and is in no mood to invite anyone in. Where Whittemore reads the White House's part in the Huang affair as the public gaining a say, Zitron reads it as cronyism: the President rescuing a brittle industry to steady the stock market. He says the episode has made people take sides, and that it "only prolongs the inevitable" because the money is running out. For him, whether AI is a bubble is no longer an open question to be discussed politely.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is who now disciplines the AI industry: the public and its politics, or the money. Both accept as fact that the President intervened at Nvidia, that the market rallied, and that the intervention headed off a repricing of the industry; Whittemore says that is partly why people are upset. The empirical question is whether wider scrutiny produces any constraint. The observables are the congressional hearings and whether AI shares hold their post-rescue gains. The residue is worldview: whether a sceptic is someone to persuade or someone already proved right. For Whittemore to be vindicated, public involvement must produce workable rules and demand must keep pace with the build-out. For Zitron, funding must tighten whatever the conversation. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is their agreement that the rescue postponed a reckoning. Watch whether the hearings lead to anything binding.
